doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Learning piano: neighborhood teachers, Bill Franks and advice to young players
summary: Largely self-taught after early beginner teachers, he credits Bill Franks's Teddy Wilson style and freedom, and urges young players to study classical technique and go to New York.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: So from hearing these records and then deciding that this is something that I want to try to do, how did you teach yourself how to play jazz?

Well I pretty much did myself. I had a series of, I started early studying which was fortunate, at about seven, but generally it was neighborhood piano teachers which in those days there was a piano teacher in almost every block, you know it was very common, part time piano teachers. There were pianos in most homes, or many homes anyway, and it was much more common to find pianos in someone’s living room. And so I studied with a series of okay beginning teachers. But I’ve always regretted I never had one that was really a real task master, a real disciplinarian, because later on I had to go back and kind of re-teach myself a lot of things, correct a lot of bad habits that I had gotten away with early. But at least I did have the advantage of having started early. But really as far as whatever technical facility I have is pretty much self taught. I made myself later try to learn how to do it right or as best I could. But I did have one teacher, a man who was not particularly interested in teaching scales and Chopin etudes tunes or anything of that nature, but he was a Teddy Wilson fan and he played in that style, and played very well in that style. He had a great left hand stride style and the wonderful time feel and all. And I finally got with him when I was about twelve or thirteen. His name was Bill Franks and he’s since deceased but he taught here for many years. And he was marvelous. Each week we would take songs and just reharmonize them. And he was marvelous at allowing a student the freedom to try things. And he would be encouraging, he would never say no you can’t do that because it’s not right. There was no right or wrong. He would just say well that’s interesting. And then maybe if you tried this it might even be better. So that was a very positive input. But I used to take some really crazy ideas each week, a re-thinking of “Stardust” or something that I’m sure he was probably cringing some of that time at my attempts, but it was a wonderful opportunity for a young player to learn through someone like that. So anyway basically I am a self- taught player with a lot of help from this one particular teacher.

Well this was really before — I was interested in classical music but it was slightly later that I became interested in that aspect of music. But today it’s such a different situation with so much jazz education and the young players today, so many of the pianists I hear, I mean they sound like conservatory-trained players, I mean as far as pure facility is concerned. Wonderful chops and they’ve obviously had — at least they sound to me as though they’ve had very, very good strong training. And that’s another thing I try to encourage young players, I don’t really teach, but if I do talk with a young player I always try to stress well whatever style you want to play, whatever you want to do as far
as jazz is concerned, get with a good classical teacher and learn how to really play the instrument. And they don’t always want to hear that but — and then, go to New York.
They could say, yeah, well watch Thelonious Monk playing.
Well I know, sure. And it’s hard to answer that.
But you say he’s Monk and you’re not.
